## Section 2: Ideas That Could Work (100)

### Data (1–20)

# 1. Full-synthetic "textbook curriculum" corpus
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.11644)
- Generate the entire pretraining corpus with a frontier model as a graded K-12-to-undergrad textbook series: definitions, worked examples, exercises, solutions. No raw web at all. Maximizes facts-per-token for a model that can only afford ~2B unique tokens.

# 2. WRAP-style rephrase everything 4 ways
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.16380)
- Rephrase each source document into 4 registers (textbook, QA pairs, dialogue, summary). Same facts, multiple surface forms — teaches the knowledge, not the phrasing, and multiplies effective dataset size.

# 3. Fact-density filtering
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.05405)
- Score every document by named entities + verifiable claims per 100 tokens; train only on the top slice. With ~2 bits/param capacity, every low-density token is wasted budget.

# 4. Train a 10M-param data filter ensemble
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.11794)
- DCLM showed model-based filtering wins. At our scale we can afford to validate filters empirically: train 10M proxy models on candidate data slices, keep filters whose slices yield the best proxies.

# 5. Knowledge-graph-to-text generation
- (idea)
- Walk Wikidata triples, render each entity neighborhood as fluent text in several phrasings. Guarantees uniform coverage of core world facts instead of web data's popularity skew.

# 6. Spaced-repetition data scheduling
- (idea)
- Show each fact-bearing document at increasing intervals during training (epoch 1, 3, 9, 27...) instead of uniform shuffling. Mirrors human memory consolidation; fights the catastrophic forgetting that hits small models hardest.

# 7. Curriculum: TinyStories → FineWeb-Edu → reasoning traces
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.07759 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17557)
- Three-stage curriculum: simple coherent language first, dense knowledge second, reasoning last. Each stage initializes the next; grammar is cheap to learn early and expensive to learn late.

# 8. Aggressive semantic dedup with one-shot exceptions
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17557)
- SemDeDup-style removal of near-duplicates, but deliberately keep 2–3 paraphrase variants of high-value facts (idea #2). Dedup junk, multiply gold.

# 9. Decay-resistant "core knowledge" replay buffer
- (idea)
- Hold out a 100M-token distilled core (definitions, math facts, common-sense assertions) and mix 5% of it into every training stage including finetuning. Anchor against forgetting.

# 10. Negative-knowledge data
- (idea)
- Include explicit "common misconception → correction" pairs. Small models hallucinate confidently; training directly on error-vs-truth contrasts may buy calibration cheaply.

# 11. Code as reasoning scaffold, even for a non-code model
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.11644)
- Include 10–15% simple Python even if code generation isn't a goal — code's explicit state and control flow measurably improves natural-language reasoning in small models.

# 12. Tool-call traces in pretraining
- (idea)
- Pretrain on synthetic traces of calculator/search/lookup tool use. A 100M model shouldn't memorize arithmetic or rare facts — it should learn to delegate. Bakes the interface in early.

# 13. Multi-hop QA chains as a first-class data type
- (idea)
- Synthesize questions whose answers require chaining 2–3 facts that appear in separate documents, with the chain spelled out. Forces knowledge-composition circuits a small model won't form on its own.

# 14. Definition-first vocabulary injection
- (idea)
- For every token in the tokenizer vocab, include dictionary-style definition + example sentences. Guarantees no token is undertrained — a known failure mode in small models with big vocabs.

# 15. Compression-as-filtering
- (idea)
- Use gzip/LLM-perplexity agreement to drop both incompressible noise and trivially compressible boilerplate; keep the mid-band where information lives. Cheap, scalable, model-free first pass.

# 16. Self-correction traces from teacher failures
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/html/2504.14523v1)
- Collect cases where a mid-size model errs and a frontier model corrects it; train on the full error→critique→fix trace. Teaches recovery behavior, which matters more for weak models than strong ones.

# 17. Domain-stratified token budget
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.05405)
- Allocate the token budget explicitly (e.g., 40% general knowledge, 20% reasoning, 15% code, 15% dialogue, 10% math) and enforce per-domain dedup, rather than letting web priors set the mix. At fixed capacity, the data mix IS the model spec.

# 18. Frontier-model "exam writing" for eval-driven curation
- (idea)
- Have a frontier model write thousands of exam questions per domain; measure checkpoint accuracy per domain; reweight next data mix toward weak areas. Closed-loop data curriculum.

# 19. Train on Gemma's actual outputs across a broad prompt set
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531)
- The target is "close to Gemma E4B quality" — so make Gemma the data generator: millions of prompts, sampled Gemma responses as targets. Direct behavioral cloning of the reference model.

# 20. Long-tail amputation
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.05405)
- Deliberately exclude rare entities (below a Wikipedia pageview threshold) from pretraining and route those to retrieval (idea #41). Don't spend scarce bits on facts almost no user will ask.

### Architecture (21–40)

# 21. Deep-and-thin baseline: ~40 layers, ~512 width
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14905)
- MobileLLM's central finding applied to 100M: maximize depth at fixed budget. Start near 40 layers × 512 dim with GQA and tied embeddings; ablate from there.

# 22. Looped middle block (2–4 iterations)
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.03819 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05171)
- Keep unique entry/exit layers, loop the middle stack 2–4 times with shared weights. Effective depth 60+ at the parameter cost of ~20 layers.

# 23. Adaptive loop count at inference (latent test-time compute)
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05171)
- Train the looped block with stochastic iteration counts so inference can dial 1–8 loops per difficulty. A 100M model that loops 8x on hard questions rents compute instead of owning parameters.

# 24. Factorized embeddings (ALBERT-style)
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.11942)
- Project vocab → 128-dim → model-dim. With a 32k vocab and 512 width, tied factorized embeddings free ~10M+ params for transformer layers.

# 25. Over-tokenized input, small output vocab
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/html/2501.16975v1)
- Large n-gram-augmented input embedding (cheap: lookup only) with a small output softmax. Gets the documented input-vocab gains without paying output-projection compute.

# 26. Byte-level fallback hybrid tokenizer
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.09871 and https://arxiv.org/html/2501.10322v2)
- Small ~16k subword vocab plus byte-level composition for rare words (hierarchical byte→word encoder). Shrinks embedding table while staying robust to typos and rare strings.

# 27. Per-layer LoRA deltas on a shared block
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.12880)
- One shared transformer block + tiny per-iteration LoRA adapters. 95% of weights shared, but each "layer" can still specialize. Best of ALBERT and standard stacks.

# 28. Product-key memory layer for facts
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.01178)
- Replace one mid FFN with a product-key memory (millions of sparse slots, O(√N) lookup). Sparse memory stores facts far more cheaply per-bit than dense FFN weights — the highest-leverage swap for "stuffing info in."

# 29. Tiny MoE: 8 experts of 8M, top-2 routing
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/html/2605.27358v1)
- ~100M total params but only ~40M active per token. More stored knowledge at the same inference cost; the same trick (per-layer expert routing) that makes Gemma E4B punch above its active-parameter count.

# 30. SSM/attention hybrid for long context on the cheap
- (idea)
- Replace 2/3 of attention layers with Mamba-style SSM blocks; keep a few attention layers for retrieval-within-context. Cuts KV-cache memory so the small model can afford long contexts — its substitute for parametric knowledge.

# 31. Multi-token prediction heads
- (idea)
- Auxiliary heads predicting tokens t+2..t+4 during training (dropped at inference). Documented sample-efficiency gains; free quality at zero deployed-parameter cost.

# 32. Ternary (1.58-bit) 400M ≡ fp16 100M
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09527 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.11895)
- If the constraint is really memory/deployment size, train a ~400M-param BitNet ternary model occupying the bytes of a 100M fp16 model. 4x the knowledge slots in the same footprint; use the 16-bit→1.58-bit transition schedule.

# 33. Head-wise attention sharing
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.11819)
- Share attention parameters across heads/layers where redundancy analysis shows near-duplicate heads. Reclaim those params for FFN/memory capacity.

# 34. Width-asymmetric FFN (wide early, narrow late)
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.14531)
- Early layers do feature extraction (need width); late layers refine (need depth). Taper FFN expansion ratio from 4x down to 2x across depth instead of uniform allocation.

# 35. Trained register/scratchpad tokens
- (idea)
- Prepend 16 learned "register" tokens that carry no text but give attention a persistent workspace. Nearly free parameters; documented to stabilize and improve transformer reasoning.

# 36. Entropy-gated early exit
- (idea)
- Add lightweight exit heads at 1/3 and 2/3 depth; easy tokens exit early. Saved inference compute funds more loops (idea #23) on hard tokens — compute allocated by difficulty.

# 37. Separate "knowledge neck" for retrieval injection
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.04426)
- One dedicated cross-attention layer mid-network reads retrieved passages (RETRO-lite: single layer, not interleaved). Minimal param cost; clean interface between parametric reasoning and non-parametric knowledge.

# 38. QK-norm + zero-init residual gates for deep-thin stability
- (idea)
- 40+ layer thin models are unstable; QK normalization and zero-initialized residual gates (ReZero-style) are near-free changes that keep very deep tiny models trainable at high LR.

# 39. Logit-softcap and z-loss for small-model calibration
- (idea)
- Gemma-style logit soft-capping plus z-loss regularization. Small models overconfidently spike logits; capping improves both training stability and downstream calibration for ~zero cost.

# 40. Recycled KV cache as working memory across turns
- (idea)
- Persist and re-attend to compressed KV summaries of earlier conversation turns instead of re-encoding text. Effective long-term memory for a model too small to internalize the session.

### Training & Distillation (41–70)

# 41. Reverse-KL distillation from a 4–9B teacher
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08543)
- MiniLLM-style reverse KL so our tiny student commits capacity to the teacher's modes, not its tail. Teacher: Gemma-class open model; this is the main training objective after the LM warm-up.

# 42. Ensemble-teacher distillation
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.02019)
- Baby Llama showed ensemble distillation beats any single teacher at 58M scale. Blend 2–3 diverse open teachers' distributions (after tokenizer alignment, idea #44).

# 43. Attention-relation distillation (architecture-agnostic)
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.10957)
- MiniLM-style Q-K/V-V relation matching from the teacher's last layer only — works despite our exotic student architecture (loops, MoE) because it doesn't require layer-to-layer correspondence.

# 44. Universal-logit distillation across mismatched tokenizers
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.13765)
- Optimal-transport-based logit alignment so we can distill from teachers with different vocabularies. Unlocks ensemble idea #42 without forcing one tokenizer.

# 45. On-policy distillation loop
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/html/2509.26497)
- Student generates, teacher scores/corrects each chunk, student trains on dense per-token teacher feedback. Fixes exposure bias that plain sequence distillation leaves behind; cheap because the student is tiny.

# 46. Shear-then-distill from an open 1–2B model
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06694)
- Structured-prune a strong open 1.4B down to ~100M (Sheared-LLaMA recipe), then continue with distillation. Inherits trained circuits at ~3% of from-scratch compute — likely the strongest single recipe available to us.

# 47. Massive overtraining: 100–300x Chinchilla
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.08540)
- 100M model, 200–600B tokens (multi-epoch over curated data). Loss keeps dropping predictably past "optimal"; inference cost of a tiny model makes the trade trivially worth it.

# 48. muP for hyperparameter transfer from 10M proxies
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10545v1)
- Tune LR/init/batch on 10M-param proxies under maximal-update parameterization, transfer to 100M exactly. Spends ablation compute at 1/10th cost.

# 49. WSD schedule with branched anneals
- (idea)
- Warmup-stable-decay LR: hold a stable plateau, then branch multiple cheap anneals on different data mixes from one checkpoint. Lets us A/B final-stage mixes (idea #18) without retraining the trunk.

# 50. Rationale distillation with answer-only inference
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.09629 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.11045)
- Train on teacher chain-of-thought, but also train a compressed "direct answer" mode from the same examples. Reasoning shapes the weights during training; inference stays short for easy queries.

# 51. Self-consistency-filtered synthetic targets
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.12309)
- When generating training data with a teacher, sample N solutions, keep only majority-consistent answers as targets. Cheap correctness filter that sharply boosts synthetic-data quality.

# 52. Iterative self-improvement rounds at tiny scale
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14159)
- After distillation: student generates on training prompts, a verifier (teacher or unit tests) filters wins, student trains on its own filtered wins. STaR-style loops are affordable when the student costs pennies to sample.

# 53. Continual QAT schedule if going ternary
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.11895)
- For idea #32: train 16-bit for the first ~60% of tokens, transition to 1.58-bit QAT for the rest. Documented to beat ternary-from-scratch across 11 tasks.

# 54. Knowledge-capacity checkpointing
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.05405)
- Probe checkpoints with a fixed synthetic fact-recall battery (bits stored per param) throughout training. Detects when knowledge absorption saturates — the signal to switch data stage or stop.

# 55. Curriculum temperature on teacher logits
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531)
- Start distillation at high temperature (rich dark knowledge, easy targets), anneal toward low temperature (sharp decisions) late in training. Matches target difficulty to student maturity.

# 56. Hard-example mining from student perplexity
- (idea)
- Continuously oversample training documents where student loss is high but teacher loss is low — the "learnable gap" region. Avoids wasting epochs on what's already learned or what's hopeless.

# 57. Critique-conditioned finetuning
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.19227)
- Teacher generates data tailored to observed student weaknesses (aligning teacher generation with student preferences/failures). The teacher adapts to the student, not just vice versa.

# 58. Embedding warm-start from a large model
- (idea)
- Initialize token embeddings from a strong open model's embeddings (projected down via PCA to our width). Embeddings encode enormous distributional knowledge; free transfer at step 0.

# 59. Batch-size ramp with sequence-length curriculum
- (idea)
- Start at 512-token sequences/small batches (fast, many updates), ramp to 4k/large batches late. Small models learn local structure first anyway; this matches compute spend to what's learnable.

# 60. Multi-stage distillation cascade (9B → 1B → 100M)
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.01108)
- Distill through an intermediate-size assistant rather than directly from a huge teacher. Documented "capacity gap" problem: students learn better from teachers nearer their own size.

# 61. DPO against the student's own failure modes
- (idea)
- Build preference pairs where "rejected" = actual student outputs that are fluent-but-wrong, "chosen" = teacher fixes. Targets the model's real error distribution, not generic preference data.

# 62. Replay-mixed post-training to prevent alignment tax
- (idea — builds on idea #9)
- Mix 10–20% pretraining replay into every SFT/DPO stage. Small models lose raw knowledge fastest during alignment; replay is the cheapest known mitigation.

# 63. Tokenizer fitted to the final data mix
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.20849)
- Train the tokenizer on the curated corpus itself (not generic web), optimizing tokens-per-byte on our actual distribution. Fewer tokens per fact = more facts per training step and per context window.

# 64. Grokking-friendly weight decay on algorithmic subskills
- (idea)
- Train arithmetic/logic subskills with elevated weight decay and extended steps to push past memorization into generalizing circuits (grokking regime). Small models can grok small algorithms; that's cheaper than storing all answer instances.

# 65. Loss-free load balancing if MoE (idea #29)
- (idea)
- Use bias-based expert routing balance instead of auxiliary load-balancing loss. At tiny expert sizes, aux-loss interference is proportionally larger; bias balancing sidesteps it.

# 66. Distill Gemma's refusal/safety behavior explicitly
- (idea — builds on idea #19)
- Include teacher safety responses in the distillation set. Safety behavior is product quality too, and small models won't learn it incidentally.

# 67. Two-pass reading: predict-then-reread objective
- (idea)
- For knowledge-dense documents, train pass 1 normally, then pass 2 on the same doc with higher loss weight on previously-missed tokens. Focused re-reading mimics how humans study; trivially implementable in the dataloader.

# 68. Train-time retrieval augmentation (RETRO-style) from the start
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.04426 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.00004)
- Pretrain with the retrieval neck (idea #37) active against a curated 1B-token database, so the model learns to lean on retrieval instead of memorizing. Retro-li proves this works at small scale.

# 69. Gaussian-noise regularization on retrieved neighbors
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.00004)
- Retro-li's trick: noise the neighbor embeddings during training so retrieval use is robust to imperfect/domain-shifted databases at deployment.

# 70. Checkpoint soup of anneal branches
- (idea — builds on idea #49)
- Weight-average the best 3–5 anneal branches (different final data mixes) into one model. Model souping is nearly free and reliably adds a point or two when branches share a trunk.

### Inference & System (71–85)

# 71. Best-of-N with a tiny learned verifier
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/html/2411.19477v1)
- Sample N answers, rank with a 20M-param verifier head trained on correctness labels. Test-time scaling laws say quality grows predictably with N — rented intelligence for a model too small to own it.

# 72. Self-consistency voting for math/logic only
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.12309)
- Route detected math/logic queries to k=8 sampled chains with majority vote; everything else greedy. Spend test-time compute only where it's known to pay.

# 73. Retrieval database as the knowledge store, model as the reasoner
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.04426)
- Ship the model with a compressed, curated ~1GB local database (Wikipedia + references). Division of labor: 100M params of language/reasoning + external facts ≈ a much larger model's effective knowledge.

# 74. Speculative self-drafting via early-exit
- (idea — builds on idea #36)
- Use the model's own early-exit head as the draft model for speculative decoding against its full-depth pass. One model, faster decoding, no second network.

# 75. Confidence-routed escalation to a big model
- (idea)
- Calibrated uncertainty head decides per-query: answer locally or escalate to an API model. The honest version of "close to Gemma quality": match it on the 80% the small model can do, delegate the rest, measure the routing rate.

# 76. KV-cache quantization to fund longer context
- (idea)
- 4-bit KV cache lets the small model hold 4x context in the same memory — and context is the small model's main substitute for parametric knowledge.

# 77. Prompt-engineered system persona tuned for the model's limits
- (idea)
- Ship a default system prompt that steers toward the model's strengths (concise answers, asks clarifying questions, cites retrieval). Free quality; small models are disproportionately steerable by prompts they were post-trained with.

# 78. Per-domain adapter packs
- (idea)
- Tiny LoRA packs (1–2M params each) for domains like medical, legal, code — hot-swapped at inference based on a classifier. The base model stays general; specialization is loaded on demand instead of stored permanently.

# 79. Structured-output grammar constraints
- (idea)
- Constrained decoding (JSON schema, grammar) at inference. Small models gain disproportionately from pruning invalid continuations — the sampler does work the weights can't.

# 80. Iterative refinement mode (draft → critique → revise)
- (idea — builds on idea #16)
- Post-train an explicit revise-own-draft behavior; at inference, run 2 passes on hard queries. Sequential test-time compute that the self-correction training data (idea #16) directly enables.

# 81. Loop-count as a user-facing "thinking" dial
- (idea — builds on idea #23)
- Expose latent-loop iterations as low/medium/high thinking effort. Same weights, graded quality-latency tradeoff, mirrors frontier "thinking budgets."

# 82. Logit fusion with a cached n-gram model
- (idea)
- Interpolate model logits with a large local n-gram/kNN-LM store at inference. kNN-LM-style fusion adds factual recall without any training — the n-gram store remembers what 100M params can't.

# 83. Session memory distillation
- (idea — builds on idea #40)
- Background-summarize each conversation into structured notes the model retrieves in later sessions. Long-term personalization without finetuning.

# 84. Sparse-friendly deployment if ternary
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.05168)
- Ternary weights are naturally sparse-friendly (many exact zeros); pair 1.58-bit weights with 2:4 semi-structured sparsity kernels for another ~1.5x speedup at deployment.

# 85. Eval harness mirroring Gemma E4B head-to-head
- (idea)
- Continuous benchmark suite scoring our checkpoints against Gemma E4B on identical prompts (MMLU, GSM8K, ARC, HellaSwag, IFEval, human preference). "Close to Gemma" must be a measured number per capability, not a vibe — and it feeds the data loop (idea #18).

### Wildcards & Research Bets (86–100)

# 86. Hash-embedding vocabulary compression
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.09871)
- Replace the embedding table with hashed compositional embeddings (each token = sum of k shared hash-bucket vectors). Cuts embedding params 5–10x; spend the savings on depth.

# 87. Curriculum-grown depth (progressive stacking)
- (idea)
- Train 12 layers, duplicate to 24, continue, duplicate to 48. Progressive stacking historically cuts pretraining cost ~25–40% and suits deep-thin targets (idea #21).

# 88. Knowledge neurons audit + targeted re-injection
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.05405)
- Probe which fact categories the final model lost; generate focused synthetic data for exactly those holes; brief repair finetune with replay (idea #62). Treat knowledge as an inventory with restocking.

# 89. Latent chain-of-thought compression
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05171)
- Distill teacher token-level CoT into the student's loop iterations (continuous latent reasoning) instead of generated text. Thinking without paying output tokens — risky but high payoff at small scale.

# 90. Tokenizer-free character model for the last mile
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/html/2501.10322v2)
- Hierarchical byte→word model variant as a parallel bet: perfect robustness to typos/casing/rare strings, zero embedding table. If BLT-style patching works at 100M, it wins the parameter budget war.

# 91. Modular two-tower: language core + swappable knowledge bank
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.01178)
- 70M "language/reasoning core" + 30M sparse memory bank (idea #28) trained to be re-writable post-hoc (memory editing). Update facts after shipping without touching the core.

# 92. Train-time dropout of retrieval to force dual competence
- (idea — builds on idea #68)
- Randomly disable retrieval for 30% of training so the model works degraded-but-sane offline, and learns what it does/doesn't know (improves routing idea #75).

# 93. Distill from a reasoning-RL teacher's pruned traces
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.24945)
- Take R1-style teacher reasoning traces, prune redundant steps with the teacher itself, distill the minimal trace. Sub-billion reasoners (MobileLLM-R1) prove the ceiling is higher than assumed; trace length is the bottleneck for tiny students.

# 94. Synthetic "society of mind" dialogues
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.01663)
- Generate multi-agent debate transcripts (proposer/critic/judge) as training data so a single small model internalizes the critic role. CMAT-style collaboration distilled into one network.

# 95. Anti-curriculum on noise tolerance, late
- (idea)
- Last 5% of training: reintroduce noisy/messy real text (typos, OCR errors, informal chat). Pure clean curated data leaves a brittleness gap with real users; sand off the distribution mismatch at the end.

# 96. Bit-level knowledge accounting dashboard
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.05405)
- Operationalize the 2-bits/param law: running estimate of facts-stored vs. capacity throughout training, per domain. Decide data-mix changes from measured capacity utilization, not intuition.

# 97. Dual-objective: LM loss + contrastive fact-retrieval loss
- (idea)
- Auxiliary contrastive head pulls representations of (question, supporting-fact) pairs together during pretraining. Doubles use of the same tokens: generation skill + retrieval-quality embeddings (serves ideas #73/#82) from one model.

# 98. Genetic/evolutionary merge of specialized variants
- (idea — builds on idea #70)
- Train short specialist branches (math, code, chat) off the trunk, then evolutionary-search merge weights (evolutionary model merging) rather than uniform souping. Finds nonlinear merge recipes souping misses.

# 99. Overtrain a 50M twin as the ablation oracle
- (idea — builds on https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.08540 and https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10545v1)
- Maintain a half-scale twin trained identically; run every risky intervention there first at 2x speed. Reliable-scaling results say 50M→100M deltas transfer; this is our cheap crystal ball.

# 100. The "knowledge sommelier" pipeline: every token earns its place
- (idea — synthesis of #1–#20)
- End-to-end gate: every candidate training document must pass fact-density (#3), dedup (#8), model-based filter (#4), and marginal-utility scoring against current checkpoint weaknesses (#18) before entering the mix. At 100M params, data admission is the product decision — run it like one.

The web search returned several highly relevant results about on-policy distillation (OPD) for large language models focusing on reasoning and scaling small models with RL techniques. Here are the key findings:

## Main Research Paper

The primary paper appears to be "Rethinking On-Policy Distillation of Large Language Models: Phenomenology, Mechanism, and Recipe," which discusses how to incentivize reasoning in LLMs through reinforcement learning.

## Key Work on Scaling Small Models

A notable study is "JustRL: Scaling a 1.5b llm with a simple rl recipe" by He et al. (2025a), available at arxiv.org/abs/2512.16649. This work obtains JustRL-DeepSeek-1.5B through RL applied to R1-Distill-1.5B.

## On-Policy Distillation Applications

OPD has been adopted in production pipelines by major models including Qwen3, DeepSeek-V4, Gemma 2, and MiMo-V2-Flash. OPD has been extended to scalable self-distillation, where a single model acts as its own teacher by conditioning on privileged information such as ground-truth solutions or execution feedback.

## Technical Insights

Research shows that the teacher's per-token log-ratio constitutes an implicit reward, and scaling this reward beyond its standard weight can push the student past the teacher's performance boundary.

The search results indicate this is an active research area with both foundational theoretical work and practical industrial implementations for improving reasoning capabilities in smaller language models through on-policy distillation and reinforcement learning techniques.

Based on the search results, here are some recent findings on tiny language models and new techniques from arXiv in 2026:

## Probabilistic Tiny Recursive Models

Tiny Recursive Models (TRM) solve complex reasoning tasks with a fraction of the parameters of modern large language models (LLMs) by iteratively refining a latent state and final answer. A recent advance is Probabilistic TRM (PTRM), a task-agnostic framework for test-time compute scaling that addresses this limitation through stochastic exploration.

## Innovative Training Techniques

Innovative techniques such as byte-level tokenization with a pooling mechanism, weight tying, and efficient training strategies are being explored for super tiny language models. Future works will explore various subproblems, including tokenizer-free models, self-play based training, and alternative training objectives.

## Task-Aware Retrieval Systems

A lightweight retrieval-augmented framework performs task-aware routing to select specialized retrieval strategies based on the input query. This approach demonstrates that smaller models can be effective when combined with smart retrieval mechanisms.

## Compression and Optimization Techniques

More broadly, TLMs are created by employing techniques such as knowledge distillation, pruning, quantization, and specialized architectures designed to minimize model size and memory footprint.

Based on the search results, here are some of the best new LLM pretraining research papers from 2026 published on arXiv:

## Notable 2026 LLM Pretraining Papers

**daVinci-LLM: Towards the Science of Pretraining**
The foundational pretraining phase determines a model's capability ceiling, as post-training struggles to overcome capability foundations established during pretraining, yet it remains critically under-explored. daVinci-LLM occupies this unexplored intersection, combining industrial-scale resources with full research freedom to advance the science of pretraining, adopting a fully-open paradigm that treats openness as scientific methodology.

**Procedural Pretraining: Warming Up Language Models with Abstract Data**
This paper shows that pretraining language models on well-chosen abstract procedural data complements standard pretraining, accelerating training and improving performance on natural language, code, and informal mathematics.

**Output Embedding Centering for Stable LLM Pretraining**
This work addresses training instabilities in large language model pretraining, specifically tackling output logit divergence that often occurs at the end of training.

**LLM Pretraining Shapes a Generalizable Manifold: Insights into Cross-Modal Transfer to Time Series**
This paper explores whether language-pretrained transformers can become effective time-series forecasters.

**Accelerating LLM Pre-Training through Flat-Direction Dynamics Enhancement**
This research focuses on adaptive optimizers as the cornerstone of modern LLM pre-training, refining the preconditioner beyond simple element-wise scaling of AdamW.

These papers represent recent advances in understanding and improving the fundamental pretraining process for large language models.

Based on the search results, here are some notable recent transformer architecture improvements and attention mechanisms from 2026:

## Historical Attention Vision Transformers

One innovation introduces a historical attention propagation methodology that preserves and integrates self-attention matrices across sequential encoder layers. This approach elevates baseline ViT accuracy on CIFAR-100 from 75.74% to 77.07% (+1.33%) and improves TinyImageNet performance from 57.82% to 59.07% (+1.25%).

## Transformer Architecture Evolution in 2026

The Transformer remains foundational for frontier models like Claude, GPT-4o, and Gemini 1.5 Pro, but has evolved into a sophisticated engine optimized for scale, speed, and massive context windows. Recent improvements include FlashAttention-3 with optimized GPU kernels for faster attention and RoPE (Rotary Positional Embeddings) allowing models to extrapolate to context windows of 1M+ tokens.

## Hourglass FFN Architecture

Researchers are revisiting transformer shape conventions by replacing the narrow-wide-narrow FFN with a hourglass FFN (wide-narrow-wide sub-MLPs), achieving comparable performance to conventional designs up to 1B parameters.

## Efficiency Improvements

While the transformer architecture has quadratic complexity bottlenecks in self-attention with respect to sequence length, architectural efficiency improvements seek to redesign parts of the model to reduce computation or memory without losing performance.

I found several relevant arXiv papers from 2026 on data-efficient training and learning from fewer tokens. Here are the key findings:

## Learning from Latents Rather Than Tokens

A key paper titled "Learn from your own latents and not from tokens: A sample-complexity theory" addresses how generative models achieve remarkable performance but require training data orders of magnitude larger than biological learners, proposing an alternative paradigm where networks are trained to predict their own latent representations of related views or masked regions, as in data2vec and JEPA. These results establish that learning from one's own latents can yield huge sample-complexity gains over token-level objectives.

## Multi-Token Prediction Methods

A paper on "Efficient Training-Free Multi-Token Prediction via Embedding-Space Probing" notes that Large Language Models possess latent multi-token prediction abilities despite being trained only for next-token generation, introducing a training-free method that enables parallel future-token prediction without modifying weights.

## Token Reduction Approaches

Another study proposes formulating token reduction as a learnable compression mapping and introduces a data-efficient training paradigm capable of learning optimal compression mappings with limited computational costs.

A method called ReGATE combines static and dynamic difficulty signals to create an adaptive, parameter-free sparsity mechanism that gates both text and vision tokens without modifying the underlying model architecture.

These papers collectively show significant progress in achieving better performance with fewer tokens through latent prediction, efficient compression, and selective token processing.

input.new_string:
### Recent Papers (2025–2026)

# IMU-1: Sample-Efficient Pre-training of Small Language Models
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.02522
- A validated, modern recipe for sample-efficient small-LM pretraining: combines data-centric strategies with current architectural and optimization advances into one tested pipeline. The closest thing to a 2026 cookbook for exactly our project.

# Nemotron-Flash: Towards Latency-Optimal Hybrid Small Language Models
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.18890
- NVIDIA's hybrid attention/SSM small-model family designed for latency-optimal inference. Current best practice for mixing state-space blocks with attention at small scale — directly informs our hybrid layer ratio.

# Rethinking On-Policy Distillation of Large Language Models: Phenomenology, Mechanism, and Recipe
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.13016
- Dissects why on-policy distillation works: the teacher's per-token log-ratio acts as an implicit reward, and scaling that reward beyond standard weight can push the student PAST the teacher's boundary. Changes distillation from imitation into something closer to RL.

# A Survey of On-Policy Distillation for Large Language Models
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.00626
- Maps the OPD landscape now used in production by Qwen3, DeepSeek-V4, Gemma 2 and others, including self-distillation where the model teaches itself by conditioning on privileged info (ground-truth solutions, execution feedback). Our post-training menu.

# Self-Distilled Reasoner: On-Policy Self-Distillation for Large Language Models
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.18734
- Single model acts as its own teacher by conditioning on privileged information, then distilling that conditioned policy into the unconditioned one. No big teacher needed for part of the pipeline — big deal for cheap iteration.

# Probabilistic Tiny Recursive Model
- https://arxiv.org/html/2605.19943v1
- Tiny Recursive Models solve hard reasoning tasks with a tiny fraction of LLM parameters by iteratively refining a latent state; PTRM adds stochastic exploration for task-agnostic test-time compute scaling. Strongest current evidence that tiny + recursion competes with big + feedforward.

# Tiny Autoregressive Recursive Models
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.08082
- Brings the recursive-refinement paradigm to autoregressive generation at tiny scale. The bridge between TRM-style puzzle solvers and an actual usable tiny LM — directly relevant to our looped-block plans.

# daVinci-LLM: Towards the Science of Pretraining
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.27164
- Fully-open industrial-scale study of pretraining science; core claim: pretraining sets the capability ceiling that post-training can't overcome. Justifies spending most of our effort and compute on the pretraining mix, not the finetune.

# Procedural Pretraining: Warming Up Language Models with Abstract Data
- https://arxiv.org/html/2601.21725v2
- Pretraining first on abstract procedural data (synthetic structured sequences) accelerates later training and improves natural language, code, and math. A cheap stage-0 warm-up we can generate for free before spending real tokens.

# Output Embedding Centering for Stable LLM Pretraining
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02031
- Fixes output-logit divergence late in training via centering of output embeddings. Stability tricks matter disproportionately for our deep-thin, heavily-overtrained setup.

# Compress-Distill: Reasoning Trace Compression for Efficient Knowledge Distillation
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05988
- Compress teacher chain-of-thought traces before distilling: students keep up to 96% of raw-trace accuracy at up to 18x better per-token efficiency. Exactly how to fit reasoning distillation into a tiny student's budget (this month's paper).

# Reasoning Compression with Mixed-Policy Distillation
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08776
- Mixed-policy distillation cuts reasoning token usage up to 27% while improving benchmark scores on a 1.7B model. Shorter thinking that's also better — the right target for small reasoners.

# Towards Efficient Large Language Reasoning Models via Extreme-Ratio Chain-of-Thought Compression
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.08324
- 73%+ CoT token reduction with slightly improved accuracy on MATH-500 at 1.7B scale. Confirms most reasoning tokens are redundant — train the student on the distilled minimal chain.

# Revisiting the Shape Convention of Transformer Language Models
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.06471
- Challenges the standard narrow-wide-narrow FFN: hourglass FFN (wide-narrow-wide) matches conventional designs up to 1B params. Fresh evidence the default block shape isn't sacred — free design space at our scale.

# Memorization Dynamics in Knowledge Distillation for Language Models
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.15394
- Distilled models memorize >50% less training data than standard finetuning while keeping capability. For us: distillation stores generalizable knowledge more efficiently per parameter than direct training — exactly the trade a 100M model needs.

# The Rise of Parameter Specialization for Knowledge Storage in Large Language Models
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.17260
- Identifies MLP value vectors as fundamental knowledge-storage units and tracks how parameters specialize for knowledge concepts. The mechanistic handle for auditing and targeting what our tiny model stores (feeds our knowledge-accounting ideas).

# What Makes Diffusion Language Models Super Data Learners?
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.04071
- Diffusion LMs extract far more learning per token than autoregressive models under multi-epoch training — analyzed mechanisms include any-order modeling and built-in data augmentation. For a data-starved tiny model doing 100 epochs, a diffusion or hybrid objective is a serious contender.

# Learn from your own latents and not from tokens: A sample-complexity theory
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27734
- Theory showing latent self-prediction objectives (JEPA/data2vec style) yield huge sample-complexity gains over token-level losses. Points to auxiliary latent-prediction losses as a way to squeeze more learning from the same tokens.

# µP-scaling Small Models: Principled Warm Starts and Hyperparameter Transfer
- https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10545v1
- 2026 treatment of maximal-update parameterization specifically for small models: warm starts plus exact hyperparameter transfer from cheap proxies. Upgrades our tuning pipeline from folklore to principle.

# JustRL: Scaling a 1.5B LLM with a Simple RL Recipe
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.16649
- Shows a deliberately simple, stable RL recipe takes a 1.5B distilled model to strong reasoning without exotic tricks. Evidence that the post-distillation RL stage for small models can be simple and cheap — don't over-engineer it.

# Pedagogically-Inspired Data Synthesis for Language Model Knowledge Distillation
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.12172
- Generates distillation data using teaching principles (scaffolding, worked examples, difficulty progression) rather than raw teacher sampling. Direct upgrade to our synthetic-curriculum data ideas.

# LoopFormer: Elastic-Depth Looped Transformers for Latent Reasoning via Shortcut Modulation
- https://arxiv.org/html/2602.11451v1
- 2026 looped-transformer design with elastic depth: shortcut modulation lets one shared block run a variable number of latent reasoning iterations efficiently. The modern version of the looped-middle-block idea we planned.

# Small Language Models (SLMs) Can Still Pack a Punch: A Survey
- https://arxiv.org/html/2501.05465v2
- Recent survey focused specifically on where SLMs match or beat larger models and which techniques got them there. Good cross-check that our chosen technique stack matches what actually worked.

- https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.13016
- Dissects why on-policy distillation works: the teacher's per-token log-ratio acts as an implicit reward, and scaling that reward beyond standard weight can push the student PAST the teacher's boundary. Changes distillation from imitation into something closer to RL.

# A Survey of On-Policy Distillation for Large Language Models
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.00626
- Maps the OPD landscape now used in production by Qwen3, DeepSeek-V4, Gemma 2 and others, including self-distillation where the model teaches itself by conditioning on privileged info (ground-truth solutions, execution feedback). Our post-training menu.

# Self-Distilled Reasoner: On-Policy Self-Distillation for Large Language Models
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.18734
- Single model acts as its own teacher by conditioning on privileged information, then distilling that conditioned policy into the unconditioned one. No big teacher needed for part of the pipeline — big deal for cheap iteration.

# Probabilistic Tiny Recursive Model
- https://arxiv.org/html/2605.19943v1
- Tiny Recursive Models solve hard reasoning tasks with a tiny fraction of LLM parameters by iteratively refining a latent state; PTRM adds stochastic exploration for task-agnostic test-time compute scaling. Strongest current evidence that tiny + recursion competes with big + feedforward.

# Tiny Autoregressive Recursive Models
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.08082
- Brings the recursive-refinement paradigm to autoregressive generation at tiny scale. The bridge between TRM-style puzzle solvers and an actual usable tiny LM — directly relevant to our looped-block plans.

# daVinci-LLM: Towards the Science of Pretraining
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.27164
- Fully-open industrial-scale study of pretraining science; core claim: pretraining sets the capability ceiling that post-training can't overcome. Justifies spending most of our effort and compute on the pretraining mix, not the finetune.

# Procedural Pretraining: Warming Up Language Models with Abstract Data
- https://arxiv.org/html/2601.21725v2
- Pretraining first on abstract procedural data (synthetic structured sequences) accelerates later training and improves natural language, code, and math. A cheap stage-0 warm-up we can generate for free before spending real tokens.

# Output Embedding Centering for Stable LLM Pretraining
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02031
- Fixes output-logit divergence late in training via centering of output embeddings. Stability tricks matter disproportionately for our deep-thin, heavily-overtrained setup.

# Compress-Distill: Reasoning Trace Compression for Efficient Knowledge Distillation
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05988
- Compress teacher chain-of-thought traces before distilling: students keep up to 96% of raw-trace accuracy at up to 18x better per-token efficiency. Exactly how to fit reasoning distillation into a tiny student's budget (this month's paper).

- https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.15394

- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.04071

- https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27734
- Theory showing latent self-prediction objectives (JEPA/data2vec style) yield huge sample-complexity gains over token-level losses. Points to auxiliary latent-prediction losses as a way to squeeze more learning from the same tokens.

- https://arxiv.org/html/2602.10545v1
- 2026 treatment of maximal-update parameterization specifically for small models: warm starts plus exact hyperparameter transfer from cheap proxies. Upgrades our tuning pipeline from folklore to principle.

- https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.16649

# Pedagogically-Inspired Data Synthesis for Language Model Knowledge Distillation
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.12172
- Generates distillation data using teaching principles (scaffolding, worked examples, difficulty progression) rather than raw teacher sampling. Direct upgrade to our synthetic-curriculum data ideas.

# LoopFormer: Elastic-Depth Looped Transformers for Latent Reasoning via Shortcut Modulation
- https://arxiv.org/html/2602.11451v1
- 2026 looped-transformer design with elastic depth: shortcut modulation lets one shared block run a variable number of latent reasoning iterations efficiently. The modern version of the looped-middle-block idea we planned.

I found several relevant papers from 2026 related to hierarchical recursive latent reasoning architectures for small models. Here are the key results:

## Main Papers Found:

1. **Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM)**: The Hierarchical Reasoning Model first demonstrated that extremely small models could achieve remarkable performance on abstract reasoning through latent recursion, with only 27M parameters achieving 40.3% on ARC-AGI-1.

2. **Tiny Recursive Model (TRM)**: The Tiny Recursive Model proposed a simplified architecture that achieves even stronger performance with fewer parameters (5–7M). TRM is a simple recursive reasoning approach that achieves strong generalization on hard tasks using a single tiny network recursing on its latent reasoning feature and progressively improving its final answer.

3. **Generative Recursive Reasoning (GRAM)**: GRAM is a framework that turns recursive latent reasoning into probabilistic multi-trajectory computation, which differs from deterministic approaches by enabling multiple solution paths.

4. **Recursive Inference Machines**: This work conceptualizes reasoning as the iterative refinement of a latent state through a structured Solver-Generator-Reweighter loop.

These papers represent recent advances in enabling small neural networks to perform complex reasoning tasks through hierarchical, recursive latent space computation.

I found several relevant arxiv papers about hybrid state space models and linear attention architectures for language models from 2026. Here are the key findings:

## Recent Hybrid Architecture Papers

Hybrid State-Space models combine Attention layers with recurrent State-Space Model (SSM) layers. While Attention stores every past token verbatim in a Key-Value (KV) cache that grows linearly with context length, each SSM layer maintains a fixed-dimensional latent state that contains a compressed summary of the entire past. The resulting hybrid architecture balances two complementary forms of memory: eidetic memory from Attention, which retains tokens exactly at quadratic cost, and fading memory from SSMs, which compresses history into a fixed-size state at linear cost.

## Benefits of Hybrid Approaches

The hybrid architecture yields a smaller KV cache, faster decoding, and a richer design space than pure Transformers. Hybrid architectures have gained adoption as a balanced approach—retaining a portion of Softmax Attention in the model to maintain both efficiency and expressive power.

## Notable Recent Works

The search results reference several 2026 papers including:
- "Priming: Hybrid State Space Models From Pre-trained Transformers" (arxiv:2605.08301)
- Papers on distillation to hybrid architectures 
- Analysis of functional components in hybrid language models

These papers represent the current state of research in combining linear-complexity sequence models with selective attention for improved language model performance.

### Unique Architectures

# Less is More: Recursive Reasoning with Tiny Networks (TRM)
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04871
- A single 5–7M parameter network recursing on its own latent state beats far larger models on hard reasoning (ARC-style). Successor to the 27M Hierarchical Reasoning Model (40.3% ARC-AGI-1). The most extreme existence proof that recursion substitutes for parameters.

# Tiny Recursive Models on ARC-AGI-1: Inductive Biases, Identity Conditioning, and Test-Time Compute
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.11847
- Dissects WHY TRM works: which inductive biases, conditioning tricks, and test-time compute settings carry the performance. The ablation map to read before building anything recursive.

# Tiny Recursive Reasoning with Mamba-2 Attention Hybrid
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.12078
- Merges the two hottest tiny-model directions: TRM-style latent recursion with a Mamba-2/attention hybrid backbone. Basically a prototype of the architecture class we should be considering at 100M.

# Recursive Inference Machines for Neural Reasoning
- https://arxiv.org/html/2603.05234
- Reasoning as iterative latent-state refinement through a structured Solver–Generator–Reweighter loop. A more modular take on recursion: separate roles inside the loop rather than one undifferentiated block.

# GRAM: Generative Recursive Reasoning
- https://arxiv.org/html/2605.19376v1
- Turns recursive latent reasoning probabilistic: multiple stochastic solution trajectories instead of one deterministic refinement path. Gives recursion a best-of-N flavor inside latent space — test-time scaling without output tokens.

# Prototype Transformer: Towards Language Model Architectures Interpretable by Design
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11852
- Replaces self-attention with learned prototype vectors; linear in sequence length, scales well with model/data size, competitive on generation and GLUE. Interpretable-by-design AND cheaper — unusual combo worth a small-scale ablation.

# Modeling Next-Token Prediction as Left-Nested Intuitionistic Implication
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.19915
- Derives a neural architecture from proof theory: next-token prediction as nested intuitionistic implication, realized as a low-rank multiplicative RNN. The weirdest entry here — but principled derivations sometimes find structure brute-force search misses.

# Priming: Hybrid State Space Models From Pre-trained Transformers
- https://arxiv.org/html/2605.08301v1
- Converts pretrained transformers into attention/SSM hybrids instead of training hybrids from scratch. Pairs perfectly with our shear-then-distill plan: take a pruned transformer, prime it into a hybrid, keep the trained knowledge.

# Hybrid Linear Attention Done Right: Efficient Distillation of Hybrid Models
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.22156
- The 2026 recipe for distilling transformer teachers into linear-attention hybrid students correctly — which layers to keep softmax, how to transfer attention behavior. Removes most of the risk from going hybrid.

# Hybrid Architectures for Language Models: Systematic Analysis and Design Insights
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.04800
- Systematic sweep of attention/SSM mixing ratios, placements, and memory tradeoffs (eidetic KV memory vs. fading SSM state). The design table for choosing our hybrid layout instead of guessing.

# Effective Distillation to Hybrid xLSTM Architectures
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.15590
- Distills transformers into xLSTM-based hybrids — the forgotten third option beyond attention and Mamba. Fixed-state recurrence with exponential gating; strong fit for low-memory deployment.

# Energy-Based Diffusion Language Models for Text Generation
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.21357
- Full-sequence energy model on top of each diffusion step — joint correction of whole sequences rather than token-by-token commitment. Interesting for small models, which suffer most from early-token error cascade.

# Coevolutionary Continuous Discrete Diffusion: Make Your Diffusion Language Model a Latent Reasoner
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.03206
- Couples continuous latent reasoning with discrete diffusion generation; shows a T-depth looped transformer implicitly simulates T-step chain-of-thought. Connects diffusion's data-efficiency to latent recursion — both of our big bets in one frame.

# Every Attention Matters: An Efficient Hybrid Architecture for Long-Context Reasoning
- https://arxiv.org/html/2510.19338v1
- Hybrid layout tuned specifically for long-context reasoning quality, not just throughput. Relevant because long context is a tiny model's substitute for parametric knowledge — we need the hybrid that preserves reasoning over it.

---

## Section 2: Ideas That Could Work (100)

content.text:
Added "Unique Architectures" subsection — 14 papers, file now 72 total.

Four architecture families found:

1. **Tiny recursive reasoners** — strongest signal for us. TRM: 5–7M params beating big models on ARC via latent recursion; plus its ablation study, a Mamba-2 hybrid version, Recursive Inference Machines (structured Solver–Generator–Reweighter loop), and GRAM (stochastic multi-trajectory recursion).

2. **Attention/SSM hybrids** — Priming (convert pretrained transformer→hybrid, fits our shear-then-distill plan), Hybrid Linear Attention Done Right (distillation recipe), systematic design-space analysis, xLSTM hybrids, Every Attention Matters (long-context reasoning layout).

3. **Diffusion/energy text models** — Energy-Based Diffusion LM (whole-sequence correction), Coevolutionary Continuous-Discrete Diffusion (diffusion + latent reasoning combined).

4. **True oddballs** — Prototype Transformer (attention replaced by prototype vectors, linear cost, interpretable), proof-theory-derived multiplicative RNN.

Biggest takeaway: tiny-recursion line (TRM family) is most direct evidence for sub-100M intelligence — parameters traded for iteration.

Sources: [TRM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04871), [TRM on ARC-AGI](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.11847), [TRM Mamba-2 Hybrid](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.12078), [Recursive Inference Machines](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.05234), [GRAM](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.19376v1), [Prototype Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11852), [Intuitionistic Implication LM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.19915), [Priming](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.08301v1), [Hybrid Linear Attention](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.22156), [Hybrid Systematic Analysis](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.04800), [xLSTM Distillation](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.15590), [Energy-Based Diffusion LM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.21357), [CCDD](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.03206), [Every Attention Matters](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.19338v1)

)

content.text:
Mined the chat. Lots of signal. Findings:

## Ideas already brewing in your Discord (MythosMini-relevant)

**Architecture**
1. **Looped/recurrent-depth transformer with depth-wise LoRA** — Glint's actual design: 4 prelude layers → 1 shared block looped 4× with per-loop LoRA rank-8 → 4 coda layers. 9 unique blocks, 12 effective depth. Matches research.md ideas #22/#27 almost exactly — the chat independently converged on it.
2. **Looping tradeoff noted by Dragonoid**: looping boosts reasoning but hurts memorization — and that's fine because RAG supplies facts externally and tiny models can't memorize anyway. Clean argument for looped-core + retrieval split.
3. **moon_senpai's gated-deltanet (GDN) hybrid** — keeping linear attention even though standard attention wins at 75M, because the 75M is a validation run for a 0.9B with 128k context. "Looped GDN" came up too.
4. **canitdotts: "attention on attention + mixture of lookup key-value experts"** — cited [arxiv 2410.20672](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.20672) and [arxiv 2512.09723](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.09723) (Mixture of Lookup Experts). Core pitch: "100M active, 350B knowledge" — extra params are per-layer lookup embeddings, not weights; "essentially the model is doing RAG internally." Same family as Gemma's per-layer embeddings (E4B is really ~8B because PLE doesn't count as active).
5. **Ternary upscaling distillation** — canitdotts: distill an fp16 teacher into a ternary student that's *larger* than the teacher; param increase just fills the memory savings. Matches research.md idea #32, plus chat's claim that ternary matches BF16 past ~3B.
6. **QAT format inventions**: "4.58-bit" (int4 plus a true structural zero — int4 weights + learned sparsity mask, ~4.2 bits/weight), and FP4 with learned per-layer exponent bias (each layer learns where its 16 codepoints sit; tiny meta-net predicts shifts). Both original, untested, cheap to ablate.
7. **Model growing** — moon_senpai: train sub-100M preview, then grow it (Net2Net-style, cited [arxiv 1511.05641](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.05641); "Oros was trained that way"). Matches research.md idea #87 (progressive stacking).

**Training**
8. **"Recursive STM"** — Glint's measured result: re-feed full dataset to a model that already "graduated"; accuracy jumped 45%→90% (another run 40%→80%) because it re-reads old data with mature representations. This is your idea #67 (predict-then-reread) with actual in-house evidence. Strongest house finding in the chat.
9. **Muon optimizer** — multiple members using it; one warning: improperly-set Muon stalled loss at 3.0. Config matters.
10. **MTP (multi-token prediction)** — used in Finnyboy's training, matches research.md idea #31.
11. **Data mix proposal (Pedro)**: FineWeb-Edu 50% / FineWeb 40% / Stack-Edu 10%; moon_senpai adds FineMath for reasoning; canitdotts objects there's not enough world knowledge in that mix.
12. **Distributed "grid" training** — pooled community hardware: ~520 TFLOPs FP16 / 2.2 PFLOPs FP8 counted. canitdotts suggestion: do QAT FP8 from step 0 since FP8 compute is 4x the FP16 pool; also split work — int4 forward on CPUs, shadow-weight/quantize-dequantize loop on GPUs.

**Data / distillation lessons (from sister channels)**
13. **Validate datasets before burning money** — Mage spent $250 on an Opus dataset whose script dropped thinking tags. Lesson: 10-row test runs first; check for empty-output rows (armand0e found "TONS").
14. **Gemini CoT poisons datasets** — Harmacist: Gemini obfuscates CoT into summaries; training on it breaks models. Filter teacher CoT by provider.
15. **Generalizing tiny models fails, specializing works** — repeated observation: 270M/1B finetunes beat ChatGPT on *narrow* tasks (classifiers, text cleaning), but broad distills drop benchmarks. Supports per-domain adapter packs (idea #78) over one generalist tune.
16. **CoT-heavy distill data ratio**: a working Claude-distill set was 65.8% CoT tokens / 34% response. Reference point for your reasoning-trace mix.
17. **Targets set in chat**: floor = beat Qwen 3.5 0.8B; stretch = Gemma 4 E4B-class; "needs to beat gemma 4 e4b at 100m class to count as a mythos implementation" — your exact goal originates there.

Biggest takeaways: **Recursive STM result (#8)** is real in-house data worth formalizing; **mixture-of-lookup-experts/PLE (#4)** is the most direct path to "100M active, way more knowledge" — and it's exactly how Gemma E4B itself cheats.

Want these folded into research.md as a third section (community ideas + the two arxiv links)?

# 100. The "knowledge sommelier" pipeline: every token earns its place
- (idea — synthesis of #1–#20)
- End-to-end gate: every candidate training document must pass fact-density (#3), dedup (#8), model-based filter (#4), and marginal-utility scoring against current checkpoint weaknesses (#18) before entering the mix. At 100M params, data admission is the product decision — run it like one.

---

## Section 3: Community Ideas (from the MythosMini Discord)

# C1. Looped recurrent-depth core with depth-wise LoRA (Glint's design)
- (community — Glint Research)
- The in-house architecture already sketched: 4 prelude layers → 1 shared block looped 4× with per-loop LoRA rank-8 → 4 coda layers. 9 unique blocks, 12 effective depth. Independently converges with ideas #22/#27 — strong sign this is the right backbone family.

# C2. Looping trades memorization for reasoning — and that's fine
- (community — Dragonoid)
- Observation from looped-model experiments: looping improves reasoning but hurts memorization. Argument: irrelevant at tiny scale because (1) RAG supplies facts at runtime, (2) a tiny model can't memorize much anyway. Clean justification for looped-core + retrieval division of labor (pairs with #73).

# C3. Mixture of Lookup Experts / per-layer embeddings: "100M active, 350B knowledge"
- https://arxiv.org/html/2512.09723 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.20672
- (community — canitdotts) Most of the parameters are per-layer lookup embeddings (an internal database), not active weights — "essentially the model is doing RAG internally." Same mechanism as Gemma's PLE: E4B is really ~8B total but only ~4B active. The most direct route to our target, because it's literally how the target model cheats.

# C4. Ternary upscaling distillation: student BIGGER than teacher
- (community — canitdotts; pairs with idea #32)
- Distill an fp16 teacher into a ternary student with MORE parameters than the teacher — the param increase just fills the memory saved by 1.58-bit weights. Chat also notes ternary matches BF16 quality past ~3B params; upscaling may buy that back at small scale.

# C5. "4.58-bit" format: int4 plus a true structural zero
- (community — canitdotts)
- Int4 lacks ternary's exact-zero sparsity. Proposal: int4 weights + learned sparsity mask — 16 values plus structural zero, ~4.2 bits/weight at 80% density. Untested, cheap to ablate at our scale.

# C6. FP4 QAT with learned per-layer exponent bias
- (community — canitdotts)
- Each layer learns its own E2M1 exponent shift — effectively learning where to place its 16 codepoints on the real line (dense near zero vs. wide dynamic range), with a tiny meta-network predicting per-layer shifts. Main network trains entirely in FP4.

# C7. Model growing: train sub-100M preview, then grow it
- https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.05641
- (community — moon_senpai; pairs with idea #87) Net2Net-style function-preserving growth: validate small, then expand parameters and continue training. Claimed precedent: "Oros was also trained that way." Lets us ship a preview model and scale the same run later.

# C8. Recursive STM: re-feed the full dataset after "graduation"
- (community — Glint Research, measured in-house)
- Re-introducing the complete dataset to an already-trained model spiked accuracy 45%→90% (another run 40%→80%) — the model re-reads old data with more sophisticated representations. In-house evidence for the predict-then-reread idea (#67); formalize and ablate round 3.

# C9. Gated DeltaNet (GDN) hybrid attention, kept for scaling headroom
- (community — moon_senpai)
- Keep linear-attention GDN layers even though standard attention wins at 75M, because the small model validates an architecture meant to scale (0.9B, 128k context). Also floated: "looped GDN" — recursion over a linear-attention core.

# C10. Muon optimizer — with config discipline
- (community — multiple members)
- Several members training with Muon successfully; one cautionary tale of misconfigured Muon stalling loss at 3.0. Use it, but validate the config on a 10M proxy first (pairs with #48).

# C11. Community data mix: FineWeb-Edu 50 / FineWeb 40 / Stack-Edu 10 (+FineMath)
- (community — Pedro, moon_senpai, canitdotts)
- Concrete starting mix proposed in-channel; FineMath added for reasoning. Open objection: not enough world knowledge in that mix — which is exactly what C3/retrieval should cover.

# C12. Validate distillation datasets before spending
- (community — hard lesson, $250 burned)
- A teacher-data run silently dropped thinking tags and produced unusable data; other sets had many empty-output rows. Rule: 10-example dry run, schema validation, and output-presence checks before any large generation job.

# C13. Filter teacher CoT by provider — obfuscated CoT poisons training
- (community — Harmacist)
- Gemini returns summarized/obfuscated CoT rather than true reasoning; training on it degrades models. Only distill reasoning from teachers that expose genuine CoT, and verify by reading samples.

# C14. Specialize, don't generalize, at tiny scale
- (community — repeated observation)
- Broad distills onto 1B models dropped benchmarks, while narrow finetunes (classifier, text-cleaner on 270M) beat ChatGPT on their task. Supports per-domain adapter packs (#78) over a single generalist finetune for capability claims.

# C15. CoT-heavy distill ratio reference point: ~66% thinking tokens
- (community — Harmacist's working dataset)
- A Claude-distill set that worked in practice was 65.8% CoT tokens / 34.2% response tokens. Use as the starting ratio for reasoning-trace data before tuning (interacts with Compress-Distill-style trace compression).

Glint Research: Yes — the embedding table is literally an nn.Embedding(vocab_size, dim), which is a vocab_size × dim weight matrix. Every row is a learned parameter. And since the output head is weight-tied ([model.py line 679](file:///home/lane/MyTrainer/model.py#L678-L679): self.head.weight = self.embed_tokens.weight), adding one token adds exactly dim parameters (128 for haiku), not 2 × dim.
So for haiku with vocab ~110 tokens and dim=128, the embedding table alone is ~14K params. If you doubled the vocab to 220, that's another ~14K params — meaningful when your whole model is ~1M.
That's also why haiku uses character-level tokenization instead of a BPE vocab of 32K+ like GPT — a 32K × 128 embedding would be 4M params, larger than the rest of the model combined.

Glint Research: Yes — the embedding table is literally an nn.Embedding(vocab_size, dim), which is a vocab_size × dim weight matrix. Every row is a learned parameter. And since the output head is weight-tied ([model.py line 679](file:///home/lane/MyTrainer/model.py#L678-L679): self.head.weight = self.embed_tokens.weight), adding one token adds exactly dim parameters (128 for haiku), not 2 × dim.
So for haiku with vocab ~110 tokens and dim=128, the embedding table alone is ~14K params. If you doubled the vocab to 220, that's another ~14K params — meaningful when your whole model is ~1M.
That's also why haiku uses character-level tokenization instead of a BPE vocab of 32K+ like GPT — a 32K × 128 embedding would be 4M params, larger than the rest of the model combined.

kyr0: Trivial graphs work, but it is not better than asking an LLM for obvious things right now. The magic is in compression. I want it to generalize better and trace reasoning deeper. The benefit of neurosymbolic AI is that it isn't merely softmax() after MLP and Attention and what not. It's not a purely stochastic system. It is more deduction than induction. It's like: From A follows B because of C. And it doesn't go wrong. It's always deduced correctly. The problem is mainly that once graphs grow, context window grows massively and likewise I cannot add infinite layers. So Attention Residuals may help me with this and I'm working on QAT for quantization aware training.. and some tricks with keeping the KV Cache small. It's a hard nut to crack
kyr0: No, it starts with the tokenizer. You don't model language. You model logical symbols, data and knowledge references. # C15. CoT-heavy distill ratio reference point: ~66% thinking tokens
- (community — Harmacist's working dataset)
- A Claude-distill set that worked in practice was 65.8% CoT tokens / 34.2% response tokens. Use as the starting ratio for reasoning-trace data before tuning (interacts with Compress-Distill-style trace compression).

# C16. RYS ("Repeat Yourself"): find the reasoning layers and repeat them
- (community — canitdotts, Dragonoid)
- Locate the layers doing reasoning in a trained model and duplicate/loop them (like the old 4x-Llama-3B passthrough merges), then finetune so the model learns to use the extra passes. Glint's caveat: untrained looping breaks the model — the finetune step is mandatory. Cheap post-hoc depth.

# C17. RL-in-the-middle distillation cascade: 1T → 1B (RL'd) → tiny
- (community — Glint Research, Dragonoid; extends idea #60)
- "Train 1B models, RL them good and tidy, then distill into tiny models." The intermediate model is not just smaller — it's RL-polished first, so the tiny student inherits post-RL behavior instead of raw teacher sampling.

# C18. CoT → latent reasoning curriculum
- (community — Dragonoid, Glint; in-house signal)
- Start training with explicit text CoT, then gradually shift to latent reasoning by feeding intermediate thoughts back as input embeddings. Glint attributes a measured quality jump in a tiny model to adding latent reasoning. The training-schedule version of Coconut/recurrent-depth (pairs with #89).

# C19. Scale the tokenizer to the model, not the convention
- (community — Glint, LH-Tech, Dragonoid)
- Worked math from the chat: at 1M params a 32k-BPE embedding table (4M params) is bigger than the whole model — so char-level wins there; a 500-token BPE worked for a 0.5M model; bigger vocabs only as the param budget grows ("100M could afford a whole-word tokenizer"). Vocab size is a first-class architecture knob at our scale, traded directly against depth.

# C20. Fully-synthetic non-grounded model: reasoning core, facts via tools
- (community — Amy; extreme version of ideas #1/#20)
- 350M trained from scratch on purely synthetic abstract-reasoning and conversation data — deliberately NOT grounded in world knowledge, which comes from tools/RAG at runtime. Skips normal pretraining entirely (procedural data only). The maximal "don't spend params on facts" bet.

# C21. Community MoE recipe data point: 412M, 3 routed experts, 262k vocab
- (community — model-card plan shared in-channel)
- A documented next-step recipe from a member's reproducible-tiny-model line: 412M MoE with 3 routed experts, 262144 vocabulary, distillation pretraining from frontier teachers, token budget past Chinchilla. Useful as a concrete comparison spec one notch above our budget.

# C22. Neuron-as-mini-MoE with internal expert types
- (community — Glint experiment)
- Each unit routes among three internal experts: a standard expert (counting/patterns), a log-space math expert (products/physics), and a key-value "vault" expert for exact fact recall — plus an internal thought loop that re-routes hard problems back through itself. Micro-scale version of routing + memory + recursion in one block.

# C23. Neurosymbolic deduction sidecar for hallucination control
- (community — kyr0)
- Auxiliary tiny model with a *defined* (not learned) tokenizer of a few hundred logical symbols, modeling knowledge-graph cause→effect deduction in latent space rather than language. Paired with an SLM as a tool, it supplies verified deductions and knowledge references — "it doesn't go wrong; it's always deduced correctly." Compression of the graph, not text, is the hard part.

# C24. Retro-fit CoT into CoT-less distill datasets
- (community — Mage; flagged as risky)
- Use a second model to inject synthetic reasoning traces into teacher datasets that lack CoT. Consensus: likely jank if naive, but viable if injected CoT is verified for answer-consistency first (combine with self-consistency filtering, idea #51).

# C25. Distill-data hygiene rules (TeichAI server lessons)
- (community — armand0e, Harmacist)
- Field-tested rules: deduplicate prompts across all combined datasets (many sets share prompt pools); drop competitive-coding data when LoRA-tuning (real-world prompts work, contest code hurts); a real capability boost needs billions of quality tokens — small SFT sets only shift style; raw teacher traces (e.g. gpt-oss-120b) train fine while summarized CoT doesn't (see C13).

# C26. Inference defaults matter for distilled students: top_k=0
- (community — Harmacist)
- A distilled model behaved much more reliably with top_k disabled. Distilled tiny models have sharper, teacher-shaped distributions; aggressive truncation samplers fight that. Ship recommended sampler settings with the model.

# C27. Target reasoning-style spec for distillation data
- (community — shared style spec)
- Define the CoT style you distill, not just the content: "a living stream of consciousness with explicit low-level self-audit embedded in natural inner narration — notices ambiguity, distrusts easy intuitions, verifies intermediate steps." A written style spec keeps multi-teacher reasoning data consistent.

# C28. Tiny-model training data points from the community
- (community — assorted)
- Calibration anchors from real runs: Supra Mini 8M = 5B FineWeb-Edu tokens × 2 epochs; Glint's recurrent 1M trained on FineWeb-Edu + uniformly-reformatted SFT sets; a 145B-token FineWeb-Edu pretrain at small scale. Useful when sanity-checking our own token budgets.

# C29. Agent-swarm research harness with central experiment memory
- (community — canitdotts)
- Meta-idea for running the project: a toggleable swarm of agents generates hypotheses/plans, a centralized harness holds the memory of all experiments and results; alternate swarm-planning phases with training/testing phases and feed results back. Research-ops, not architecture — but it compounds every other idea here.
